title: 2024–2026 operating and capital budget approved
subtitle: Infrastructure funding trimmed, fire hiring phased, arts funding boosted, school-zone sidewalk clearing rejected.
overview: Council approved a three-year budget for 2024 to 2026. The average property tax increase is 6.14% in 2024 {{vote:m65}}, 6.34% in 2025 {{vote:m66}} and 6.41% in 2026 {{vote:m67}}, with a 2024 levy of $99,609,666. A 2024–2026 capital budget of $363,019,000 was also approved {{vote:m63}}.

To lower the increase, council trimmed planned infrastructure reserve contributions {{vote:m20}}, deferred some new staff start dates to June, raised investment income targets, and asked staff to find $100,000 in savings by 2026 {{vote:m39}}. Winter sidewalk maintenance enhancements go ahead, with their cost smoothed over three years {{vote:m27}}. Motions for sidewalk clearing in all school zones and for a sustainability officer failed.

Council added $30,000 a year for not-for-profit cultural funding and asked staff to report by December 2024 on sustainable support for arts and creative industries. City utilities budgets and debenture financing were also approved.

decisions.detail: Council approved the 2024 budget with an average property tax increase of 6.14% and a levy of $99,609,666 {{vote:m65}}; the 2025 and 2026 budgets were approved in separate motions.
Council approved the 2024–2026 capital budget of $363,019,000 and approved the 2027–2033 forecast in principle.
Council approved debenture financing of up to 10 years for projects including Beaver Creek Road reconstruction, fire rescue expansion, water and stormwater work, and a $10,000,000 facility project.
Council approved reductions in ongoing funding for 2024 to 2026 under the revised fire-related budget item {{vote:m19}}.
Council reduced the planned increase in infrastructure reserve funding for 2024 {{vote:m20}}, with matching reductions for 2025 and 2026 in later motions.
Council added $30,000 for not-for-profit cultural sector funding, paid from Council's Community Priority and Contingency Reserve.
Council approved a new Transportation Engineering Supervisor position starting in 2026 {{vote:m31}}.
Council directed staff to increase revenues or reduce expenses by $100,000 over three years, with the savings applied to the 2026 budget {{vote:m39}}.

debate: A delegate argued that low-cost, high-impact services such as sidewalk snow clearing add little to the tax bill, and that the biggest tax pressures come from outside the city's control.
Another delegate urged council to return the budget to staff or approve only 2024. Staff said multi-year budgeting saves staff time, helps secure grants and lets tenders go out early.

Several councillors opposed cutting infrastructure funding, citing the share of assets in poor condition and the higher cost of delaying work. Supporters of the cut said the public wants lower tax increases.

On sidewalk clearing in school zones, councillors and staff questioned the cost and whether the city should clear the sidewalks in front of private homes. Some also said school boards already clear their own frontage. The motion failed.

A proposed deferral of library funding failed. A library representative said the library could absorb a one-year cut from its reserve, but some councillors said the library already does a lot with its funding.
